title: Build and operate intelligent apps with Microsoft Fabric: New capabilities at Ignite 2026
author: shireesht

content.text:
If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric.
AI-powered development tools are making it faster than ever to build applications. But moving from prototype to production remains challenging. Developers still need to connect applications to enterprise data, secure access, manage databases, and ensure applications can operate reliably at scale.
At Microsoft Ignite, we're introducing new capabilities in Microsoft Fabric that bring application development, operational databases, and database management closer together, helping teams build and operate intelligent applications with less complexity.
We are announcing three important milestones toward that vision:
• Fabric apps (Generally Available), helps developers and coding agents build and deploy complete business applications with enterprise data, security, and governance built in, using the open-source Rayfin SDK and CLI.
• Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB (Preview), brings serverless PostgreSQL to Fabric for the dynamic workloads of modern applications and AI agents.
• Database Hub in Fabric (Generally Available), provides a unified experience to discover, monitor, and manage databases, with database agents for SQL and PostgreSQL now in preview.
Together, these innovations simplify the journey from idea to production and bring greater intelligence to database operations.
Move from prompt to production with Fabric apps
Fabric apps (Generally Available), give developers and coding agents a simpler path to building and deploying complete business applications.
Developers and coding agents can build Fabric apps with Rayfin, the open-source SDK and CLI that provides backend capabilities including databases, authentication, functions, storage, and observability. When deployed to Fabric, these applications become Fabric apps, connecting application experiences with enterprise data and governance in Microsoft Fabric. Since launching in preview just five months ago, more than 100,000 Fabric apps have been created.
Figure: Animated GIF - Examples of data-rich business applications built with Microsoft Fabric apps.
Build on trusted enterprise data
Fabric apps connect to existing semantic models, warehouses, and lakehouses, allowing developers to build on trusted business data without recreating data models or access controls. Teams can extend analytics into interactive applications that support business workflows, enabling users to move from understanding what's happening to taking action.
With general availability, we're also introducing enhanced security and governance capabilities. A new Apps view in the OneLake Governance hub gives administrators visibility into applications across their organization, with the ability to block or unblock them. Content Security Policy settings and private sites provide additional protection.
We're also making it easier to build Fabric-powered applications from the tools people already use. With Microsoft Copilot, builders can go from a simple prompt to a working application, with the option to use Fabric as a ready-to-use data backend for databases, storage, and data APIs. Integrations with Power BI Desktop will also help teams turn trusted semantic models into interactive business applications.
Customers are already seeing the potential.
“Rayfin aligns closely with Hitachi Energy’s long-term vision for a unified data, analytics, and AI platform built on Microsoft Fabric. Rayfin provides a compelling way to move beyond traditional reporting and deliver Fabric-native operational experiences that bring together data, insights, and business processes.”
—Niek Brasa, Chief Architect at Hitachi Energy
Learn more about the new capabilities and how to get started in the Rayfin and Fabric apps blog post.
Serverless PostgreSQL in Fabric, built for intelligent applications
Developers have always built applications on databases, but agents are now building them at an entirely different speed. Agents spin up databases for prototypes, experiments, and short-lived tasks, then drop them when the work is done. Most of these workloads start small, run in bursts, and sit idle between uses, which makes their compute needs hard to predict and inefficient to run continually.
Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB is serverless and built for exactly these scenarios, with:
• Rapid provisioning: Databases provision in seconds so developers and agents can start building immediately.
• Automatic pause: Compute pauses after five minutes of inactivity to avoid keeping resources running between tasks.
• On-demand resume: Compute resumes when the next query arrives without manual intervention.
Fabric HorizonDB is also available as a PostgreSQL database for Fabric apps. Its serverless architecture gives developers and coding agents a database that can be provisioned quickly, scales with application demand, and pauses when not in use, without requiring them to manage the underlying infrastructure.
Once those applications are running, they need more than their own operational data. Fabric HorizonDB now supports translytical capabilities on OneLake to operationalize lake data, bringing the scale and performance of Fabric's analytical engines to live transactions through:
• Translytical queries: PostgreSQL queries are transparently converted to run on Fabric Data Warehouse, using distributed, scale-out execution on CPU- or GPU-powered processing. Analytical queries can run an order of magnitude faster or more than they would natively in PostgreSQL. Full and partial pushdown are both supported, so a single query can join PostgreSQL tables with data in OneLake.
• Mirroring: Fabric HorizonDB tables are replicated into OneLake by default and are automatically converted to Delta format, so data is ready for translytical application workloads and large-scale analytics across Fabric without building data integration pipelines.
• Synced Tables: Enriched data from Fabric Data Warehouse flows back into HorizonDB (reverse ETL) for low-latency, high-concurrency serving to applications and agents. Snapshot sync handles periodic refreshes such as daily scores or aggregates, while the continuous sync option keeps tables current as source data changes.
Figure: Fabric HorizonDB unifies operational and analytical data through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, enabling applications to query, analyze, and act on data across Fabric and OneLake.
Together, serverless compute and translytical capabilities on OneLake give applications and agents a single PostgreSQL endpoint for working across live operational data and analytical data in Fabric. They can start small, scale with demand, and act on transactions and insights without building separate data pipelines or managing database infrastructure.
Opsen AI, for example, is exploring how these capabilities can help financial services firms respond faster to payment and trade exceptions.
“As settlement cycles shorten and financial services become more automated, resolving payment and trade exceptions requires more than the current transaction state. Fabric HorizonDB enables us to connect operational data with historical insights in OneLake to provide firms with the broader business context to resolve exceptions faster and make more informed decisions.”
— Jennings Balavari, Founder and CEO, Opsen AI
Learn more in this Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB blog post.
Simplify database management with Database Hub in Fabric
As developers and coding agents build more applications, database environments are becoming increasingly complex. Database professionals need a simpler way to manage growing database estates, monitor performance, and troubleshoot issues without switching between multiple tools.
Database Hub in Microsoft Fabric (Generally Available), provide a centralized experience to discover, monitor, and manage databases across the organization. It brings together database management and operational insights in one place, helping teams improve visibility and streamline everyday operations.
Figure: Animated GIF - How Database Hub and database agents help simplify database management with unified visibility, AI-powered monitoring, and actionable insights.
This centralized view helps database teams move beyond fragmented, reactive management toward more proactive operations.
“Managing a database estate that spans thousands of client environments across multiple servers used to mean stitching together visibility from a dozen different places. Database Hub in Fabric gives us a single pane of glass over our entire estate, so we can proactively monitor performance and security posture and know exactly where to focus. It’s transformed how we operate at scale.”
— Brian Roth, Co-Founder and CTO, Evention
Building on this foundation, we are expanding Database Hub with new capabilities that make database operations easier:
• Unified monitoring and insights: Monitor database health and performance across supported databases, identify potential issues, and uncover opportunities to optimize performance. Enhanced monitoring and alerting help teams proactively address issues before they affect applications.
• Copilot in Database Hub: Use natural language to explore database health, investigate performance issues, and get guidance on potential next steps, reducing the time spent navigating tools and interpreting diagnostic information.
• Database agents: New AI-powered agents for SQL and PostgreSQL help database professionals investigate performance and health issues. Built on Microsoft-authored skills, these agents analyze database context, suggest potential root causes, and recommend actions to help teams troubleshoot more efficiently.
Together, these capabilities help database teams move from reactive troubleshooting to more proactive database management, with greater visibility and AI-powered assistance built into their workflows.
Learn about Database Hub, database agents, and more in this Microsoft SQL blog.
Bringing applications, data, and AI together
What excites me most is how these innovations bring application development, operational databases, analytics, and AI together in Microsoft Fabric. From building apps with Fabric apps to powering them with Fabric HorizonDB and managing databases through Database Hub, we're making it easier for developers and database teams to build, deploy, and operate intelligent applications with less complexity.
Sessions you won't want to miss at Microsoft Ignite
There is much more to explore at Microsoft Ignite. Join our Fabric sessions and labs to see these capabilities in action, hear directly from the teams building them, and learn how to put them to work across your data estate. I especially encourage you to attend:
• BRK362: Data foundations for modern apps, AI, and agents
• BRK355: Build like a startup. Deploy like an enterprise
• BRK359: Build intelligent PostgreSQL apps with Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB
• BRK363: Less hunting, more building: Database agents in a unified estate
• BRK372: Where agents meet analytics: Build with SQL Database in Fabric
Get started
• Build your first Fabric app: Explore the Rayfin SDK and CLI and deploy your first Fabric app.
• Try Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB: Learn more about Fabric HorizonDB.
• Manage your database estate: Learn more about the new Database Hub capabilities.
